extracted.intended_audience: authors of book-length fiction and memoir manuscripts seeking developmental editing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and service-specification for a developmental (story-level) edit of a full manuscript: what the edit includes, how it is done, what it focuses on, exclusions, deliverables, timing, and pricing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of a developmental edit
rubrics_metrics.description: A developmental edit analyzes what makes your story work, highlighting strengths and opportunities for improvement. It hones your narrative into its most compelling form for readers in a way that matches your vision and goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to give honest, useful, constructive feedback that helps authors get 'unstuck' rather than to reassure or to rewrite for the author. Useful when an author has a finished manuscript and wants to make it as good as possible or has rewritten multiple times and needs objective, professional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two read-through process (cold read + close read)
rubrics_metrics.description: A developmental edit typically includes two read-throughs: a cold read and a close read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cold read: read the full manuscript as a reader with minimal notes, recording impressions at the end to see the shape of the story and genre relevance. Close read: detailed pass focusing on big-picture elements, ignoring spelling/punctuation/grammar, with margin notes and analytical commentary. This sequencing helps the editor form a reader's-first-impression and then a craft-based analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader response comments
rubrics_metrics.description: In-manuscript reader response comments indicate areas that are very effective and areas that are less effective from a reader's perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are explicitly subjective: they show how a reader responds to your words (what grabbed attention, built suspense, or made them care). They complement analytical editorial notes by providing reader-facing insight into emotional and engagement effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical editorial notes/comments
rubrics_metrics.description: In-manuscript editorial comments are more analytical and craft-focused than reader responses and provide suggestions and solutions to consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These comments focus on elements of writing craft (e.g., scene purpose, clarity, consistency) and are less subjective. They form the basis of the editorial report and offer actionable suggestions rather than mere impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial report considers characterisation: how well characters are drawn, developed, and whether they engage the reader and serve the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis may include critique of motivation, agency, distinctiveness of voice, character arcs, and whether characters' actions align with stakes and plot. The editor may also produce a character list to clarify cast and relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial report evaluates dialogue for realism, distinctiveness of voice, purpose, and contribution to character and plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on whether dialogue advances plot or reveals character, whether it rings true for each voice, and whether it needs tightening or expansion. Examples and suggested rewrites may be provided in editorial notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial report assesses the clarity, immediacy, and escalation of stakes throughout the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor checks whether readers understand what’s at risk, whether stakes increase appropriately, and whether stakes are tied to character goals and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial report analyzes the plot for coherence, causality, pacing, and whether scenes serve the story's central questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes identification of plot holes, redundancies, unclear causal links, and suggestions for restructuring or scene changes to strengthen narrative drive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pace
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial report examines the story's pace—how quickly or slowly the narrative moves and whether tempo suits the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor looks for scenes that lag or rush, balance between action and reflection, and overall rhythm across chapters and acts; may recommend trimming or expanding sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial report evaluates transitions between scenes and chapters for clarity and flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks whether shifts in time, perspective, or scene are signposted and smooth, and whether transitions maintain momentum or create confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description and setting/worldbuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial report considers description and worldbuilding: how setting is used to support story, atmosphere, and character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor assesses specificity vs. over-description, whether setting details serve plot or theme, and consistency of world rules; suggestions can include adding sensory detail or paring needless exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backstory
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial report evaluates how backstory is deployed—its timing, integration, and whether it supports character and plot without bogging the story down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor may suggest moving, condensing, or revealing backstory differently to maintain tension and avoid info-dumps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing vs telling
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial report considers the balance of showing and telling and whether scenes show character and stakes effectively rather than merely summarise them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations may include converting telling passages into scenes, adding sensory detail, or using action/dialogue to reveal interiority rather than exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure analysis (scene/chapter-by-chapter and overall story shape)
rubrics_metrics.description: A developmental edit includes analysis of structure, such as a chapter-by-chapter record table or a story-structure graph and scene-by-scene notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor will map story beats, identify structural weaknesses (misplaced scenes, pacing problems, arc inconsistencies), and recommend reorganisations. The choice of a table vs graph depends on what will be most helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter-by-chapter notes / scene-by-scene notes
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial deliverables often include chapter-by-chapter or scene-by-scene notes documenting purpose, problems, and suggested changes for each unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These notes aim to give actionable, granular guidance authors can apply when revising scene-level issues in service of the larger story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character list as a deliverable
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor may produce a character list summarising characters, roles, relationships, and potential confusions in cast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for identifying redundant or underused characters and clarifying viewpoint/role consistency across the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial questions and suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial report includes editorial questions for the author and concrete suggestions to consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions are used to prompt author reflection and to guide revisions; suggestions are not mandatory prescriptions but options for strengthening the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report length and verbosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Developmental editorial reports are usually 9–12 pages of precise, thoughtful commentary without being overwhelming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report length signals depth of analysis; the editor aims to be thorough yet readable, balancing detail with clarity so authors can act on recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of author-provided concerns (tailored focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor asks authors for their main concerns, questions, or difficulties and considers those carefully during the edit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailoring the edit to stated concerns ensures the report addresses the author's priorities and specific trouble spots, not only generic commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of manuscript and communications
rubrics_metrics.description: The manuscript and communications remain confidential unless the author specifically asks otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A procedural standard ensuring authors' work and privacy are protected as part of the professional service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication and collaboration cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: The service includes weekly short email updates and an introductory, feedback, and follow-up call (or email if preferred).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introductory calls help the editor hear the author's voice and understand goals; feedback and follow-up calls support iterative clarification and post-delivery support. Some calls are optional depending on the service tier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and approach of feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback is constructive and encouraging: honest about what works and what doesn't while aiming to support and educate rather than to discourage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor positions themselves as an educator (not a 'meanie'), giving frank but supportive guidance designed to motivate revision rather than to demoralise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope exclusions: not proofreading, not ghostwriting, not for reassurance-only clients
rubrics_metrics.description: Developmental editing does not address spelling, punctuation, and grammar (proofreading) and the editor does not offer ghostwriting, ghost editing, or book doctoring. Also not appropriate if the client only wants reassurance and is not open to constructive feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clients should choose other services (proofreading, line editing, ghostwriting) if they need sentence-level or rewrite work, or should not engage if they are unwilling to do revision work themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service tiers and depth-of-service distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different tiers (full manuscript developmental edit, full-manuscript developmental feedback, mini-edit developmental feedback) vary by number of read-throughs, inclusion of structural analysis, availability of follow-up calls, duration, and price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare tiers by explicit checklist: e.g., full edit = 2 reads, in-manuscript notes, full editorial report, structural analysis, weekly updates, optional calls, ~8 weeks; feedback tier = fewer deliverables and ~4 weeks; mini = 1 week, limited scope. Choose tier based on the level of analysis and time/budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turnaround time estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate durations are provided for each tier (e.g., 8 weeks for full manuscript developmental edit, 4 weeks for full manuscript developmental feedback, 1 week for mini-edit developmental feedback).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are planning estimates to set expectations about how long a thorough story-level edit will take at different service levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing and payment options
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate price ranges are given (e.g., for an 80,000-word manuscript: $2,095–$3,200 for full edit; $1,200–$2,400 for full feedback; $240–$325 for mini-edit). Payment accepted in USD, GBP, or LKR; local rates may be available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pricing communicates the resource investment required and helps authors select appropriate tier; authors should confirm currency and local rates when inquiring.
